newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scents victory in German ruling on Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scents victory in German ruling on Iran.

text.p: The United States hailed a German court finding on Thursday that Iran's leaders ordered political killings in Berlin, seeing it as a victory in its effort to persuade Europe to take a tougher line with Tehran.
"The court's verdict corroborates our long-held view that Iran's sponsorship of terrorism is authorised at senior levels of the Iranian government," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

In a later statement, Burns applauded decisions by Germany and the European Union to suspend the "critical dialogue" they have attempted to maintain with Iran for the past five years and which Washington has long branded as fruitless.
He said Washington was "very pleased" by the German and EU moves and by the German government's decision to declare several Iranian diplomats persona non grata.

"We hope that the European Union will join the United States in a realistic policy that is aimed at containing Iran and containing its ability to further destabilise the Middle East and to murder its own citizens abroad," he said.

The German court said Iran's political leadership ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant in 1992. It avoided names, but said the assassination was ordered by a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, religious leader, intelligence minister and head of foreign policy.

"The United States commends the courage of the German prosecutor, the German judges and the witnesses ... We are confident that the verdict was based on the court's objective evaluation of the evidence," Burns said.

"The United States will maintain its own sanctions on Iran and we strongly encourage our European partners to do the same," he said, adding that Washington called on Iran to "take a lesson" from the verdict and stop sponsoring "terrorism."
Tehran denies that it supports terrorism.
Iran has been a major bone of contention between Washington and its European allies.

The European Union has refused to join U.S. trade sanctions on Iran and has strongly attacked U.S. legislation providing for measures against firms that invest in the oil or gas industry in Iran or Libya.
The United States says the Europeans are motivated largely by commercial greed for deals in oil-rich Iran.
